name: Mogao Caves
info: The Mogao Caves are a system of Buddhist cave temples near Dunhuang in Gansu, China, begun in 366 CE and added to until the 14th century, known for their murals and sculptures and for the manuscripts of the Library Cave.

facts.made: Dug and decorated by Buddhist monks over about a thousand years, from the 4th to the 14th century, with funds from donors: clergy, local rulers, foreign dignitaries, Chinese emperors, merchants, officers and local families
facts.form: A system of rock-cut cave temples in a cliff close to two kilometres long, cut in soft gravel conglomerate; 735 caves survive, with murals covering 46,000 square metres and around 2,400 clay sculptures
facts.where: On the cliff 25 km southeast of the centre of Dunhuang in Gansu province, China; the Library Cave manuscripts are held mainly in Beijing, London, Paris and Berlin
facts.known: murals of Buddhas, apsaras and Pure Land paradises; the giant Maitreya statues; thousand-Buddha patterns; the Library Cave and its manuscripts; the Diamond Sutra of 868; paintings on silk; donor portraits

t: A monk named Le Zun, or Yuezun, is said to have had a vision of a thousand Buddhas at the site in 366 CE, and caves continued to be made there until the 14th century.
In 1900 the Taoist abbot Wang Yuanlu found a walled-up cave holding an estimated 50,000 documents in Chinese, Tibetan, Sogdian, Khotanese and other languages, including the Diamond Sutra of 868.
Expeditions from Britain, France, Japan and Russia removed manuscripts and paintings from 1907 to 1914, and the collections are now divided among Beijing, London, Paris, Berlin and other places.
dyk: The small seated Buddhas that cover whole walls in many caves, and give the site its common name, were drawn with stencils so that identical figures could be repeated.
ev: The monk Le Zun is said to have had a vision of a thousand Buddhas and begun the first cave
The larger of the two giant Maitreya statues, in cave 96, was constructed following the edicts of Empress Wu Zetian
Dunhuang came under Tibetan control, which lasted until 848
The Library Cave was walled up, for reasons that remain debated
Wang Yuanlu found the walled-up cave full of manuscripts
Aurel Stein removed a large number of manuscripts, paintings and textiles, followed by Pelliot in 1908
The Research Institute of Dunhuang Art, later the Dunhuang Academy, was set up at the site
The Mogao Caves became a UNESCO World Heritage Site

sections.origins:
Dunhuang was established as a frontier garrison outpost by the Han dynasty emperor Wudi in 111 BCE to protect against the Xiongnu. It became a gateway to the West, a centre of commerce on the Silk Road and a meeting place of peoples and religions, Buddhism among them. The Mogao Caves, about 25 km to the southeast, were first made in the 4th century CE, when Dunhuang was under the Former Liang dynasty.

According to Fokan Ji (An Account of Buddhist Shrines), a book written in the reign of Empress Wu Zetian by Li Junxiu, a Buddhist monk named Le Zun, which may also be pronounced Yuezun, had a vision of a thousand Buddhas bathed in golden light at the site in 366 CE and was inspired to build a cave there. The story also appears on a stele in cave 332, while another document, Shazhou Tujing (Geography of Shazhou), gives an earlier date of 353. A second monk, Faliang, joined him, and by the time of the Northern Liang a small community of monks had formed. The caves first served as places of meditation for hermit monks, then served the monasteries that grew up nearby.
sections.content:
The site is a system of about 500 temples in a cliff close to two kilometres long. Of the 735 caves that survive, the best known are the 487 in the southern section, which were places of pilgrimage and worship and are decorated. The 248 to the north were living quarters, meditation chambers and burial sites for monks, and are mostly plain. Many early caves follow the Indian chaitya plan, with a square central column representing the stupa that worshippers walk round; others are hall caves with pyramidal or gabled ceilings, and some small meditation cells follow the Indian vihara plan.

The murals cover 46,000 square metres and date from the 5th to the 14th century. Buddhist subjects are most common, but there are also traditional mythical subjects and portraits of patrons. A common motif is walls covered with rows of small seated Buddhas, with flying apsaras above and donors along the base. The paintings often show jataka tales, stories of the Buddha's lives, or avadana, parables of karma. Around 2,400 clay sculptures survive, built on a wooden frame padded with reed, modelled in clay stucco and painted, with the Buddha at the centre attended by bodhisattvas, heavenly kings and apsaras. The two giant statues, of Maitreya Buddha, have a stone core.
sections.making:
The oldest decorated caves that remain, 268, 272 and 275, were made in the Northern Liang period between 419 and 439 CE. Members of the ruling families of the Northern Wei and Northern Zhou then built many caves, and the site flourished under the short-lived Sui dynasty. By the Tang dynasty the number of caves had reached over a thousand. The local rock is a soft gravel conglomerate, unsuitable for fine carving, so the caves were finished in plaster, clay and paint rather than in stone.

Caves were made by monks as shrines, with funds from donors. The major caves were sponsored by important clergy, the local ruling elite, foreign dignitaries and Chinese emperors, and others may have been paid for by merchants, military officers and local people such as women's groups. Rich local clans built some as family caves, and their inscriptions and donor portraits stress family ties and social status. The giant northern Buddha in cave 96, 35.5 m high, was constructed in 695 after Wu Zetian ordered monasteries in 689 and giant statues in 694; the smaller southern statue, 27 m tall, was made in 713-41. Many figures used Indian shading techniques to give a three-dimensional effect.
sections.reception:
From the Sui and Tang dynasties the caves were a place of worship and pilgrimage for the public. The cave paintings and architecture served as aids to meditation, as visual representations of the quest for enlightenment, as mnemonic devices and as teaching tools for people who could not read. Early murals showed strong Indian and Central Asian influence, but a distinct Dunhuang style began to emerge under the Northern Wei, and Chinese elements increased from the Western Wei. Bodhisattvas appeared from the Northern Zhou, with Avalokitesvara the most popular, and the Sui-Tang period brought large narrative paintings of sutras and, in Tang art, the Pure Land paradise.

Under Tibetan control from 787 to 848, Dunhuang became part of an administrative system based on the Tibetan Empire, and the site escaped the persecution of Buddhists ordered by Emperor Wuzong in 845. Tantric iconography, such as the eleven-headed Avalokitesvara, became popular in this period and later. The artistry of the murals is said to have reached its high point in the Tang period, and the quality of the work dropped after the tenth century. After the Tang the site declined, and no new caves were made after the Yuan dynasty.
sections.survival:
As Islam spread across Central Asia and sea routes came to dominate Chinese trade, the Silk Road lost importance. In the Ming dynasty it was officially abandoned, and Dunhuang was gradually depopulated and largely forgotten abroad. Most of the caves were abandoned, though the site stayed a place of worship for local people. Many caves lost their wooden porches, and only five remain. A Taoist abbot, Wang Yuanlu, appointed himself guardian of some temples around 1900, and on 25 June 1900 he found a walled-up cave behind a corridor, later called the Library Cave, full of manuscripts.

Stein, in 1907, obtained around 7,000 complete manuscripts and 6,000 fragments for £130, in exchange for a donation to Wang's restoration work; Pelliot took almost 10,000 documents in 1908 for the equivalent of £90, and Otani Kozui in 1911 and Sergei Oldenburg in 1914 bought more. Scholars in Beijing then had the rest sent to Peking in 1910, though not all arrived and some were stolen. Langdon Warner removed murals and a statue in 1924, and soldiers damaged caves in 1921 and 1939. The Dunhuang Academy was founded in 1944, the caves were declared a protected monument in 1961, and they escaped the damage of the Cultural Revolution.
sections.legacy:
The Mogao Caves are the best known of the Chinese Buddhist grottoes and, with the Longmen and Yungang Grottoes, one of three famous ancient Buddhist sculptural sites in China. They became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987, and from 1988 to 1995 a further 248 caves were found north of the 487 known since the early 1900s. They are described as one of the largest repositories of Buddhist art in the world, documenting the changing styles of Buddhist art in China for nearly a thousand years.

The Library Cave documents, dated from 406 to 1002, include the Diamond Sutra of 868, the earliest dated printed book, as well as Christian Jingjiao documents, the Dunhuang Go Manual, music scores and a star map. Most are in Chinese, with others in Tibetan, Uighur, Sanskrit, Avestan, Sogdian and Khotanese, and they record Buddhism's development in China and the lives of ordinary people. The International Dunhuang Programme coordinates scholarship on them and makes them available digitally. The Dunhuang Academy began exploring digital conservation in 1993 and has photographed 120 caves since 2010. Zhang Daqian's copies of the murals, exhibited in 1943, brought their art wide attention within China.

summary: The Mogao Caves near Dunhuang are a system of Buddhist cave temples begun in 366 CE and added to until the 14th century. Their murals and sculptures record a thousand years of Buddhist art, and a sealed cave found in 1900 held manuscripts that were later dispersed to Beijing, London, Paris and elsewhere.
notes: Start date: 366 CE is the vision date in Fokan Ji; the article also gives 353 from Shazhou Tujing and says construction 'is generally taken to have begun sometime in the fourth century'; circa true.

Number of caves: the article gives about 500 temples in the lead, over a thousand at the Tang peak, and 735 surviving (487 south, 248 north); the 1980s era list sums to about 500 dated caves. Used as stated, not reconciled.

Date and reason for sealing the Library Cave are disputed (1002 per Rong 2000, early to mid-13th century per Huntington 1986, 'early 11th century' in the article); the event is given as early 11th century and the reasons are left out of the text.
The article says both 'one of the earliest' style claims (earliest dated printed book, Diamond Sutra 868) and 'earliest printed book to survive'; I used 'earliest dated printed book'.
Murals area given as 46,000 square metres (490,000 sq ft); the article also says 'half a million square feet' and '400,000 square feet' elsewhere; the metric figure used.
The great Buddha's wooden building (9 storeys, 4 originally) and the Stele of Sulaiman were left out for space; tourism and visitor caps left out per brief.
